title: Riemann Integration and Improper Integrals
breadcrumb: Mathematics → Calculus → Definite and improper integration
objectives: Explain Riemann sums and standard integrability criteria.
Evaluate definite integrals using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Define improper integrals through limits at infinite or singular endpoints.
Apply p-integral convergence criteria at zero and infinity.
Use comparison tests and split at interior singularities.

traps: A function tending to zero does not guarantee convergence.
An interior singularity requires two one-sided limits.
An antiderivative does not replace the limit.

sheet: Riemann sum: Σf(ξᵢ)Δxᵢ over a partition.
Bounded with finitely many discontinuities ⇒ Riemann integrable.
Infinite endpoint: define by lim R→∞.
Unbounded endpoint: define by a one-sided cutoff limit.
p=1 gives logarithmic divergence at both boundaries.
Interior singularity: split and test both sides separately.
Direct comparison can prove convergence or divergence.
A vanishing integrand need not have finite total integral.
tricks: Check whether the problem is proper or improper before integrating.
For infinity, use R; for a singular endpoint, use ε.
The p-threshold reverses at zero and infinity.
Use a benchmark power near the endpoint.
remember: At infinity p>1; at zero p<1.
A small tail can still have infinite area.

howto: Separate proper evaluation from convergence analysis. For improper cases, write the defining limit first, then integrate, then take the limit. Use p-integrals as benchmarks and do not merge the two sides of an interior singularity.

scenes.title: Foundation: sums, limits and accumulation

ask.q: What does ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx measure when f is non-negative?
ask.nudge: It accumulates area under the graph.

body: A definite integral accumulates function values over an interval. For a non-negative function it is area; for a sign-changing function it is signed area.
Riemann integration defines the integral through limits of finite sums. Improper integration extends the idea when an endpoint is infinite or the integrand is unbounded.

items.recall: A sum Σf(ξᵢ)Δxᵢ over a partition, with a sample point in each subinterval.
refresh: Partition the interval into small pieces. In each piece choose a sample point, multiply the function value by the width, and add the products. The result approximates the accumulated area.
When the maximum subinterval width tends to zero and the sums approach a common limit, that limit is the Riemann integral. The partition can be refined to make the approximation more accurate.

items.ask: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
items.recall: If F′=f, then ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a), under the usual continuity condition.
refresh: The theorem connects differentiation and integration. If f is continuous and F is an antiderivative, the definite integral is the difference between F at the upper and lower limits.
It also says that the derivative of the accumulation function x↦∫ₐˣf(t)dt is f(x). This is why an antiderivative evaluates a proper definite integral.

items.recall: An infinite interval or an integrand unbounded at an endpoint or interior point.
refresh: An infinite endpoint is handled by replacing it with a finite variable R and taking R→∞. An unbounded endpoint is handled by a cutoff ε approaching the singularity from inside.
An improper integral converges only if the defining limit exists and is finite. Writing an antiderivative without taking that limit is not a convergence proof.

scenes.title: Proper versus improper accumulation
scenes.objective: Recognise when a limiting process is needed.
body: A proper Riemann integral has a bounded integrand on a finite interval. Improper integrals require a limit because the interval is infinite or the integrand is unbounded.
An infinite interval can still produce finite total area. Conversely, an integrand tending to zero may have an infinite accumulated area.

ask.q: Is a bounded function with finitely many discontinuities Riemann integrable on a closed interval?

blocks.body: A bounded function is Riemann integrable when upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close by refining the partition.
Every continuous function on [a,b] is Riemann integrable. A bounded function with finitely many discontinuities is also Riemann integrable.
Boundedness is essential. An unbounded function on a finite interval may still have an improper integral, but it is not a proper Riemann integral on that interval.

steps.why: The Fundamental Theorem converts the definite integral to an endpoint difference.
The positive integrand gives a positive integral, which is consistent with 6.

scenario.teaser: A cumulative quantity is recovered from its rate.
scenario.title: Total production from a production-rate function
body: Suppose r(t) is a production rate. The total production between times a and b is ∫ₐᵇr(t)dt.
If R is an antiderivative of r, the Fundamental Theorem gives R(b)−R(a). The integral converts a rate into a cumulative amount.
This same structure appears in distance from velocity, total cost from marginal cost and probability from a density. Units provide a useful check: rate multiplied by time gives total amount.

scenes.title: Infinite-interval improper integrals
scenes.objective: Define and evaluate an integral with an infinite endpoint.

blocks.body: ∫ₐ∞f(x)dx := lim(R→∞)∫ₐᴿf(x)dx, if the limit exists and is finite.
∫₁∞x⁻ᵖdx converges iff p>1. At p=1 the antiderivative is log x and the integral diverges.
First replace infinity by R, then evaluate the proper integral, and only then take R→∞. A finite antiderivative expression at R is not yet the improper integral's value.

scenes.title: Guided: p-integral at infinity
hints: Evaluate at R and 1, then let R tend to infinity.
scenes.solution: lim R→∞[−1/(2R²)+1/2]=1/2. Since p=3>1, the p-integral converges.

ask.nudge: The truncated integral is log R.

scenes.title: Singularities at endpoints and inside
scenes.objective: Handle unbounded integrands using one-sided limits.

ask.nudge: The critical exponent is one, with the opposite inequality.

blocks.body: ∫₀¹x⁻ᵖdx converges iff p<1. At p=1 it diverges logarithmically; for p>1 it diverges more strongly.
∫₀¹f(x)dx := lim(ε→0+)∫ε¹f(x)dx, if finite. The cutoff approaches the singular endpoint from inside the interval.
If f is unbounded at c∈(a,b), split at c and require both one-sided improper integrals to converge separately.

scenes.title: Guided: singularity at zero
scenes.objective: Evaluate an improper integral near zero.
scenes.problem: Determine whether ∫₀¹x⁻¹ᐟ²dx converges and find its value.
scenes.solution: lim ε→0+[2−2√ε]=2. The exponent p=1/2 is less than one, matching the criterion near zero.

ask.nudge: Here p=2, which is not less than one.

scenes.title: Comparison tests
scenes.objective: Use standard integrals as convergence benchmarks.

ask.q: If 0≤f≤g and ∫g converges, what can be concluded about ∫f?
ask.nudge: A smaller non-negative function has no more total area.

blocks.body: For non-negative functions, 0≤f≤g and convergence of ∫g imply convergence of ∫f. If f≥g≥0 and ∫g diverges, then ∫f diverges.
If f,g>0 and lim f(x)/g(x)=L with 0<L<∞ near the improper endpoint, both integrals have the same convergence behaviour.
Near infinity compare with x⁻ᵖ using p>1. Near zero compare with x⁻ᵖ using p<1. The comparison must hold sufficiently near the problematic endpoint.

How is an interior singularity handled?
items.a: Split at the singularity and test both one-sided improper integrals.

The endpoint limit is finite and equals 2.

scenes.title: A vanishing rate may have infinite total

ask.q: Why does 1/x have a divergent integral even though it tends to zero?
ask.nudge: Its accumulated area is log R.

body: A function tending to zero does not guarantee a finite improper integral. The decay rate matters.
The area under 1/x from 1 to R is log R, which grows without bound. The faster-decaying 1/x² has a finite total area. This is the integral analogue of the harmonic versus p-series distinction.

scenario.teaser: A small rate can accumulate to an infinite total.
scenario.title: Long-run cumulative exposure
body: Imagine an exposure rate decreasing over time like 1/t. The instantaneous rate becomes small, but accumulated exposure from time 1 onward is ∫₁∞1/t dt.
That integral diverges logarithmically. A rate decreasing like 1/t² has a finite total accumulation instead.
The practical lesson is that a vanishing rate does not guarantee finite cumulative quantity. The tail must decay sufficiently fast, and the p-integral criterion makes the threshold precise.

scenes.title: Worked: an interior singularity
scenes.objective: Split an improper integral at its singular point.

ask.nudge: The integrand is unbounded at zero, inside the interval.

steps.why: Each side is a separate one-sided improper integral.
Both one-sided pieces must converge; one divergent side makes the whole integral divergent.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Every continuous function on [a,b] is Riemann integrable.
items.why: Continuity on a compact interval is sufficient.

items.claim: A function tending to zero at infinity has a convergent improper integral.
items.why: 1/x tends to zero but its integral diverges.
This is the p-integral criterion at infinity.
Near zero it converges for p<1.

items.claim: An interior singularity requires two one-sided limits.
An antiderivative alone proves an improper integral converges.
items.why: The limiting endpoint must still be finite.

scenes.title: Final integral checklist
scenes.objective: Evaluate proper and improper integrals safely.
body: 1. Proper definite integral: find an antiderivative and use F(b)−F(a).
3. Infinite endpoint: replace infinity by R and take R→∞.
4. Unbounded endpoint: replace it by ε and take ε→0 from inside.
5. ∫₁∞x⁻ᵖ converges iff p>1; ∫₀¹x⁻ᵖ converges iff p<1.
6. Interior singularity: split and test both one-sided integrals separately.
7. Use direct or limit comparison with a suitable p-integral.
